title: Blip 03 — Dialogue Voices, a Third Cast
shortText: 104 dialogue blips: 13 new speakers for school, modern and cozy games, none a Blip 01 or 02 voice. Same cues.
html:
A third cast of dialogue voices

104 dialogue sounds. 13 new speakers, each a different synthesis method.

The ticks and chirps a text box plays as a line types out, for the speakers a school, modern, cozy or visual novel game needs: a teacher, a classmate, a principal, a shopkeeper, a toddler, a cat, a voice down a phone line and a ghost in the corridor. It works on its own, and it is built to sit beside Blip 01 and Blip 02 without ever sounding like them: same 8 cues, same file names, 13 new voices.

Licence, up front

Royalty free. Commercial use. No credit required. No revenue limit, no unit cap, no second licence to buy later if your game does well. Use it in as many projects as you like, on any platform. The one thing you may not do is resell the sounds themselves as sounds. The full plain language terms ship as LICENSE.txt, with a copy paste credit line if you want one.

Everything is synthesised from code. No recordings, no sample libraries, no third party clips, so there is no upstream licence behind this one and nobody can content ID claim these sounds against your project.

Hear it first

There is a free demo on this page with four complete voices, chosen by measurement from the darkest to the brightest end of the cast, all 8 cues each, copied unaltered. Play them back to back before you pay.

The new cast

  • Principal. Deep and formal. Stacked organ tones, the lowest voice in the series. 138 Hz
  • Detective. A low voice with breath around the edges of the tone. 271 Hz
  • Grandparent. Warm and slow, with a gentle tremble in the level. 334 Hz
  • Announcer. A radio or PA announcer. A rich low tone with a studio slapback echo behind it. 617 Hz
  • Classmate. Easy going and quick. A tone that sharpens as it speaks, then softens. 815 Hz
  • Phone Call. A voice down a phone line: narrow, a little unsteady, the pitch jumping between frames. 1427 Hz
  • Shopkeeper. Quick and nasal, a voice from behind the counter. A hollow, pinched tone. 1945 Hz
  • Teacher. Clear and patient. A pulse whose width narrows through the glyph, so each one is crisp. 1989 Hz
  • Rival. Sharp and confident. A bright attack that snaps shut. 2364 Hz
  • Idol. A stage voice. Every glyph pops up a fifth, like a tiny jingle. 2376 Hz
  • Toddler. Tiny and excited. Every glyph scoops up into a squeak. 3223 Hz
  • School Ghost. A whisper that takes its time arriving. Breath and a faint tone, rising slowly. 5809 Hz
  • Cat. A house cat. The pitch rises and falls inside every glyph, bright and thin. 6180 Hz

Phase distortion, a feedback comb, a pulse width sweep, a filter pluck, drawbar organ stops, a slapback echo, a tremolo, a stepped fifth, pitch jitter in a phone band, a whisper. The figures are the mean brightness of each voice's own per glyph tick, measured off the shipped WAV files. What each description says is measured too: 20 of 20 claims hold when measured again from the files, the toddler's scoop, the idol's fifth, the announcer's echo and the rest.

Three packs, 39 voices, no collisions

Inside this pack all 78 pairs of voices are separated by at least 12 percent in brightness or 25 percent in length. Across the series the same check runs over all three casts together: 39 voices, 741 pairs, 338 of them a new voice against a Blip 01 or Blip 02 voice, and 741 of 741 are separated. The check is proven to fire: each earlier voice planted back in as a re pitched copy was caught, 26 of

  1. The result ships as series_proof.json.

Every speaker ships the same 8 cues as Blip 01 and 02

  • blip_01. tick for one glyph, take 1
  • blip_02. tick for one glyph, take 2
  • blip_03. tick for one glyph, take 3
  • soft. the same voice pitched lower, for asides and whispers
  • loud. the same voice pitched higher and held longer, for shouting and emphasis
  • question. rising inflection, for a line ending in ?
  • exclaim. emphatic hit, for a line ending in !
  • advance. page turn / next line, in this voice

File names are voice then cue, exactly as in the earlier packs, so a dialogue system already wired for Blip 01 or Blip 02 takes these voices by changing the speaker id and nothing else.

Fit

  • WAV and OGG for every file, 16 bit, 44.1 kHz, mono.
  • One loudness band. The inner 80 percent sits inside 0.41 dB, so switching speaker never changes how loud the text box is. The soft and loud cues differ in pitch and length, not level, so set their volume in your game for a real whisper or shout.
  • Slow speakers by design. Principal, Grandparent, Announcer and School Ghost tick for 150 ms or more; fire them every third glyph, or once per word.
  • 13 declared variation sets, three takes per voice, so a repeated tick never repeats a file.
  • Nothing loops, and no file carries loop points.
  • pack_proof.json ships with the pack: 945 checks, 0 failed.

Honest limits

These are synthesised character voices in the blip tradition, not recorded speech and not a vocal synthesiser. They say that someone is talking; they do not say words. The measurements above are signal measurements, not a claim that it sounds good. That is what the free demo is for.

AI disclosure, stated truthfully: the code that generates these sounds was written with AI assistance. The sounds themselves are self contained procedural synthesis, oscillators, filters and delay lines evaluated in code, with no generative audio model at any point. The cover art and store graphics are AI generated.

More voices from the same studio

  • Blip 01: Dialogue Voices for Text Advance, the first cast, fantasy speakers.
  • Blip 02: Dialogue Voices, a Second Cast, sci fi and fantasy speakers.
  • Babble 01: Dialogue Voices, speakers that talk in made up syllables instead of ticks.
